t: Maximum Number of Groups With Increasing Length
o: Build groups of sizes 1, 2, 3, ..., each group using distinct numbers, with number i usable at most usageLimits[i] times overall; maximize the number of groups. Key exchange argument: to form g groups we need 1+2+...+g = g(g+1)/2 total usages, and sorting limits ascending lets us consume cheapest capacities first. Scanning sorted limits while tracking the next required triangular number yields the greedy answer: [1,2,5] → 3 groups, [2,1,2] → 2, [1,1] → 1.
k: Feasibility of g groups depends only on total capacity versus the triangular number T_g = g(g+1)/2 when limits are consumed in sorted order.
Greedy scan: accumulate capacity; whenever it covers the next required amount (1, then 2, then 3, ...), commit one more group.
Values reach 1e9 and n 1e5, so use 64-bit accumulators.

a.i: Sort limits ascending. Maintain cur = leftover capacity and need = size of the next group. Each limit adds to cur; if cur ≥ need, we can afford the next group, so subtract and increment both counters. This is equivalent to checking partial sums against triangular numbers and is optimal by an exchange argument (using larger capacities later never hurts).
s: For each limit v: cur += v; if cur ≥ need, set cur -= need, ans++, need++.
a.t: O(n log n) — sorting dominates; the scan is linear

a.n: Approach 2: Binary Search on the Answer
a.i: Feasibility of g groups is monotone: if g groups are possible, so are g-1. Define ok(g) = the same greedy scan succeeds in committing g groups, and binary search the largest feasible g in [1, n].
s: Sort limits; write ok(g) running the greedy scan and returning whether ans reaches g.
Binary search the maximum g with ok(g) true.
a.t: O(n log n) — sorting plus O(log n) feasibility scans of O(n)

w: Present the greedy scan as the main solution — it is short and provably optimal; binary search is a nice alternative framing if you think of the answer as monotone. Pitfalls: 32-bit overflow of accumulated capacity (use long/long long), and forgetting that group sizes must be exactly 1,2,3,... (strictly increasing), not arbitrary. Follow-up: reconstruct an explicit assignment of numbers to groups.
